client: I've been really struggling since last week's team meeting, where my colleague called out some mistakes I made in front of everyone. It's been sitting with me constantly, like this heavy weight I can't shake, and I keep replaying the moment over and over in my head. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: That sounds really painful — being called out in front of your team can feel deeply humiliating, and it makes sense that your mind keeps returning to that moment trying to process it. I also notice you mentioned some doubt about whether talking will help, and I want to honor that honestly — it's okay to feel uncertain, and we can take this at whatever pace feels right for you. Can you tell me a bit more about what keeps coming up when you replay that moment — is it more about what your colleague said, how others reacted, or something else entirely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's mostly about the other people in the room, honestly. I keep picturing their faces and wondering what they were thinking about me, whether they now see me as incompetent or careless. And the worst part is I can't really ask them, so my mind just fills in the blanks and it's never anything good.
therapist: What you're describing — your mind rushing in to fill that silence with the worst possible interpretations — is actually a really common thinking pattern called mind-reading, where we assume we know what others think, and our brain almost always goes to the harshest verdict. It makes sense it feels so exhausting, because you're essentially having a negative conversation with imagined versions of your colleagues on a loop. I'm curious — if a close friend had made the same mistakes in that meeting, what would *you* have been thinking about them as you watched?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, if it were a friend, I'd probably just feel bad for them and think it was an uncomfortable situation, not that they were suddenly terrible at their job. But it feels different when it's me — like, I know my own history with mistakes and self-doubt in a way I don't know theirs, so it's hard to apply the same logic. I get what you're trying to do with that comparison, but it doesn't quite land for me the same way.
therapist: You're actually doing something really insightful there — you're not just dismissing the comparison, you're explaining *why* it doesn't quite work for you, which tells me a lot about how deep this self-doubt runs, like you hold yourself to a different standard because you're the only one who has full access to your "evidence file" of past mistakes. That inner critic has a lot of material to work with, it sounds like. I'm wondering — when you think about that history you mentioned, is this meeting starting to feel like proof of something you already feared about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, honestly, that's exactly what it feels like. Like this meeting was just confirmation of something I've always suspected — that I'm not as capable as people might think, and it's only a matter of time before everyone else figures that out too. I've never really said that out loud before and it feels kind of awful to hear myself say it.
therapist: What you just named — that fear of being "found out" — is something many people carry quietly for years, and it takes real courage to say it out loud for the first time. That belief, that you're somehow fooling people and it's only a matter of time, is actually so common it has a name: impostor syndrome, and it tends to feed on exactly these kinds of moments, treating one difficult meeting as the final proof of something that was never really true. I want to gently ask — what would it mean for you if that belief *wasn't* actually accurate?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, if that belief wasn't accurate, I think I'd feel relieved, but also kind of lost — like, that fear has been such a constant companion that I'm not sure who I am without it. It's almost like it's been motivating me in some weird way, keeping me on edge so I don't get too comfortable and slip up. I don't know if I fully trust that letting go of it would actually be safe.
therapist: What you just shared is really profound — that this fear, as painful as it is, has also felt like a kind of protection, a way of staying sharp and not dropping your guard. There's something quite tender in the way you're sitting with this, like a part of you is genuinely grieving the idea of letting it go, even while another part longs for relief. I'm curious — when you imagine "slipping up" without that fear keeping watch, what do you picture actually happening?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I picture myself becoming careless, maybe missing something important at work and then everything kind of unraveling — my reputation, my relationships with colleagues, all of it. It's like I imagine one mistake leading to this total collapse, which I know sounds extreme when I say it out loud. But even knowing it sounds extreme doesn't make the fear feel any less real in the moment.
therapist: You're already doing something really important by noticing that the fear sounds extreme even as you're describing it — that's a part of you standing slightly outside the thought and observing it, which is actually a skill. What you're describing, that one mistake leads to total collapse, is a thinking pattern called catastrophizing, where our mind skips straight to the worst possible ending without accounting for all the steps in between where things could go differently. I'm wondering — can you think of a time in the past where you did make a mistake at work, and the unraveling you're picturing... didn't actually happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: There was a time about two years ago where I sent out a report with some pretty significant errors in it, and I was convinced that was going to be the end of my credibility. But my manager just pulled me aside, we fixed it, and honestly most people seemed to forget about it within a week. I remember that, but it's strange — it doesn't really seem to stick the same way the fear does, like the evidence that things can be okay just doesn't carry the same weight as the evidence that they might go wrong.
therapist: What you just described is such a valuable piece of evidence — your brain predicted total collapse, and instead your manager handled it quietly and life moved on, which is exactly the kind of real-world data that challenges the catastrophizing story. What you're noticing about why it doesn't stick is actually one of the core things we'd want to work with — our minds have a kind of negativity bias, where threatening information gets filed away in bold and underlined, while the reassuring stuff gets stored in pencil. I'm wondering if part of what we could explore together is how to give that "pencil evidence" a little more weight — what do you think gets in the way of letting moments like that one really land for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think part of what gets in the way is that the good moments feel like luck or coincidence, like I just got away with it that time, whereas the bad moments feel like the truth finally showing through. So even when things work out, I'm not really taking credit for it or seeing it as evidence that I'm capable — I'm just relieved I wasn't caught. I'm not sure how you actually change that pattern, because it feels pretty baked in at this point.
therapist: You've just described the impostor syndrome trap so precisely — success gets filed under "luck" and mistakes get filed under "truth", which means the system is rigged against you ever really taking in evidence of your own capability. I also notice something in the way you're speaking about this, a kind of quiet tiredness, like you've been carrying this framework for a long time and part of you is worn out by it even as another part insists it's just "how things are." That sense of it feeling baked in is really worth sitting with — not because it's true, but because it tells us how long this belief has had to put down roots, and that actually helps us understand what kind of gentle, consistent work it might take to loosen it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, tired is the right word — I don't think I've ever really named it that way before, but there is something exhausting about constantly running this internal audit on yourself. I guess I'm just skeptical about what "gentle, consistent work" actually looks like in practice, because I've tried to be more positive about myself before and it always feels forced or fake, like I'm just lying to myself in a more cheerful direction. I don't want to just swap one unhelpful story for another one that's equally untrue.
therapist: Your skepticism here is actually really healthy and worth respecting — you're right that CBT isn't about replacing dark thoughts with forced positivity, because you'd see straight through that and it wouldn't hold up. What we'd be aiming for instead is something more like accuracy, training your mind to weigh evidence more fairly rather than with a thumb permanently on the scale toward the negative. I'm curious though — underneath that skepticism, I notice there's also something that sounds like a quiet longing for things to actually be different; what would it mean to you if this time, the work actually did lead somewhere real?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: If it actually led somewhere real, I think it would mean I could finally stop bracing for impact all the time — like I could just be in a moment at work without half my brain monitoring for signs that I'm about to be exposed. That sounds almost too good to be true when I say it, and I notice I'm already pulling back from it a little, like I don't want to hope for too much in case it doesn't work out. I guess that's probably the same pattern showing up again, isn't it.
therapist: You caught it yourself — that instinct to pull back just as something hopeful comes into view is exactly the same pattern, protecting you from disappointment by not letting yourself want too much, and the fact that you can see it happening in real time is genuinely significant. What you described — just being present at work without that constant internal surveillance — isn't too much to hope for, it's actually a pretty reasonable thing to want for yourself. I think that image you just painted, of being in a moment without bracing, is worth holding onto, because it gives us something real to move toward rather than just something to move away from.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
